opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a fairly common picture among the leaders of the frontier labs, and while they each put it differently, the core of it is quite similar. The emphasis tends to be on AI as a kind of superhuman scientist or researcher. Dario talks about a "country of geniuses in a datacenter," and the idea is that you have these extremely capable systems that compress decades of scientific progress, in biology and medicine for instance, into a few years. Demis has a similar emphasis. He's always framed DeepMind's mission around solving intelligence and then using it to solve science, and things like AlphaFold are the template he has in mind. Sam's framing is a bit more varied, but he also often comes back to the idea that AI will dramatically accelerate scientific discovery, and that this is where most of the value comes from.

So the shared view, roughly, is that the main channel through which AI transforms the economy is R&D: you get very smart systems, they make breakthroughs, and those breakthroughs then diffuse into everything else.

I think that picture is, if not wrong, at least quite misleading about where most of the economic value will actually come from. If you look at the economy historically, most growth hasn't come from a handful of brilliant insights. It's come from the accumulation of a huge amount of mundane work, and from scaling up the inputs to production. R&D spending is only a few percent of GDP. Most of what people do every day isn't research. It's coordinating, managing, building things, handling customers, writing code that isn't at all cutting-edge, moving physical stuff around.

Even within science, a lot of progress is bottlenecked not by having smart enough ideas but by experiments, data collection, capital, and physical infrastructure. You can have a lot of geniuses in a datacenter, but if they can't run experiments faster, build labs, or deploy what they discover, the speedup is going to be much more limited than the picture suggests.

So my view is that the bulk of the value from AI will come from broad automation of labor across the whole economy, essentially substituting AI for human workers in the huge range of tasks people currently do. That's what drives a really large increase in output, because you're effectively expanding the labor force enormously, and labor and capital can then be scaled up together. That's a very different picture from "we'll cure cancer and then good things follow." It also has different implications: it suggests the transition depends heavily on things like agency, long-horizon competence, reliability, and robotics, the unglamorous capabilities you need to actually do jobs, rather than just raw reasoning ability on hard problems.

I don't want to caricature them, because I think they'd all agree that automation of ordinary work matters. But in terms of emphasis and what they present as the headline story, I think they lean heavily toward the scientific-genius framing, and I think the broad-automation story is where most of the action really is.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts scientific discovery with broad labor automation, but does not distinguish automating AI’s own R&D from R&D across other fields.

r002.rationale: It attributes to Dario a “country of geniuses in a datacenter” and to Demis an emphasis on using AI to solve science, then describes accelerated R&D as their shared economic-value story.

r003.rationale: It says Sam often emphasizes accelerated scientific discovery, but does not mention his view that AGI might not dramatically change the world.

r004.rationale: The response mentions AlphaFold, but does not interpret AlphaGo as using reinforcement learning to develop complex reasoning.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention the GATE model or whether general-purpose R&D falls outside its scope.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's an interesting tension in how they talk about it. If you read something like Dario's "Machines of Loving Grace," or listen to Demis talk about curing diseases, or Sam talk about abundance, a lot of the framing is around what I'd call the scientific or R&D channel. The idea is that you get these very capable systems, they act like a country of geniuses in a data center, they accelerate biology, materials science, energy, and that's where the enormous value comes from. It's a story about intelligence being the bottleneck on progress and AI removing that bottleneck.

My view is that this is probably the wrong place to look for most of the economic value, at least in the near to medium term. If you look at where GDP actually comes from, it's not mostly from the output of research labs. It's from the ordinary work that hundreds of millions of people do every day: logistics, construction, retail, administration, manufacturing, services. The reason economic growth has been slow historically isn't primarily that we've lacked brilliant ideas. It's that deploying and scaling things in the physical and institutional world is hard, and it takes enormous amounts of labor and capital.

So when I think about how AI creates economic value, I think the big story is broad automation of labor. If you can substitute AI systems and eventually robots for a large fraction of what human workers do, then you've effectively made the labor supply elastic. That's what gets you the kind of explosive growth that economists like me get excited about. The research acceleration story is real, but on its own it's a much narrower channel. Even a dramatic speedup in biology still has to go through clinical trials, regulatory approval, manufacturing, distribution. Those are the slow parts, and they're slow because of people and institutions, not because of a shortage of insight.

To be fair to them, I think the lab leaders do believe in the automation story too, especially Sam, who has talked about AI agents joining the workforce. But in their public narratives they tend to emphasize the scientific breakthroughs, partly because that's more inspiring and politically palatable than saying "we're going to automate most jobs." I'd just push back on the implied model of the economy. I think they overweight the cognitive, discovery-driven picture and underweight the fact that most value creation is boring, diffuse, and labor-intensive, and that's exactly where the biggest gains from AI will come from if the technology gets good enough to actually do that work.

r002.rationale: It associates Dario’s and Demis’s public framing with AI-driven scientific breakthroughs and describes this as a source of enormous economic value.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Sam Altman’s view that AGI might not dramatically change the world.

astra-6.text:
I think there are somewhat different emphases, though I wouldn’t want to attribute a precise economic model to any of them. Dario seems to emphasize AI as a supply of highly capable cognitive labor: you could have many systems doing work that currently requires skilled people, including scientific research. The economic value comes from both doing existing tasks more cheaply and accelerating the discovery of new things.

Demis seems more focused on the scientific discovery part—using AI to solve difficult problems in biology, medicine, or other sciences. In that picture, the big payoff is the technology that AI helps us develop, rather than just automating work we already do.

Sam seems to put more emphasis on making intelligence cheap and broadly available, so that people and businesses can build useful things with it. That’s a more general-purpose platform picture, where you don’t necessarily need to predict all the applications in advance.

But these views overlap a lot. The question I’d ask of all three is how quickly improvements in AI capabilities translate into actual economic output. Being able to perform an intellectual task is one step; integrating that capability into a business, or turning a scientific discovery into a product, can require complementary investments and time. So I’d distinguish optimism about what AI can do from optimism about how quickly the economy can absorb it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions AI accelerating scientific discovery, but does not distinguish automating AI’s own R&D from R&D in other fields.

r002.rationale: It links Dario to both cheaper cognitive labor and faster discovery, and Demis to scientific discovery, but does not clearly attribute accelerating R&D as a principal value channel to both.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Sam Altman’s view that achieving AGI might not dramatically change the world.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss AlphaGo, reinforcement learning, or DeepMind’s strategy for developing complex reasoning.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention the GATE model or the scope of general-purpose R&D.

sol-6.1.text:
My impression is that they share a broad picture: AI becomes capable of doing more and more economically valuable work, and that eventually produces a very large increase in output. But they emphasize different mechanisms, and I wouldn’t assume they have identical views about how quickly that translates into economic growth.

Dario tends to emphasize systems that can perform a wide range of cognitive tasks—something like a country of very capable people in a data center. The economic value comes from being able to scale that cognitive labor, including research itself.

Demis tends to put more emphasis on scientific discovery: using AI to understand biology, develop drugs, discover materials, and solve problems that then unlock useful technologies. In that picture, an important part of the payoff comes through advances in science rather than just automating existing jobs.

Sam often talks more about making intelligence cheap and widely available. If you dramatically reduce the cost of doing intellectual work, people and businesses can use much more of it, build new products, and automate more activities.

Those are overlapping visions. The question I’d separate from all three is how rapidly capability becomes actual economic value. You still need deployment, organizational changes, and, for many applications, physical investment. Being able to solve a problem intellectually doesn’t necessarily mean you can immediately implement the solution throughout the economy.
